analysis.one_liner: Delays federal nutrition-labeling rules for vitamins, minerals, and herbal supplements until April 1994.
analysis.headline: The Senate passed the moratorium by voice vote, but the House never voted on it; its last action pointed to a different supplement bill, S.784.
analysis.plain_summary: Under the 1990 Nutrition Labeling and Education Act, the FDA was moving to require standardized labels on dietary supplements — vitamins, minerals, herbs, amino acids. This bill froze that: it barred the Secretary of Health and Human Services from implementing the act for supplements before April 15, 1994, blocked any final supplement regulations until then, and pushed back state enforcement to April 30, 1994. The Senate passed it by voice vote the day it was introduced, but the House committee never brought it up.
analysis.who_benefits: Dietary supplement makers, who would avoid the cost of printing new labels and reformulating claims for several more months, and who would gain leverage in negotiating what the final rules looked like.

how_it_helps.text: Bars the Secretary of Health and Human Services from implementing the 1990 nutrition-labeling law for dietary supplements of vitamins, minerals, herbs, amino acids, or similar substances before April 15, 1994.
Blocks the issuance of any final labeling or health-claim regulations for supplements before April 15, 1994, and deems proposed regulations not final until April 30, 1994.
Delays the effective date of state enforcement provisions for supplement labeling to April 30, 1994, so states could not step in while federal rules were frozen.
Passed the Senate without amendment by voice vote on the day it was introduced.

analysis.who_pays: Consumers who buy vitamins, minerals, and herbal products, who would go longer without standardized labels telling them what is in the bottle and what the maker claims it does.
analysis.who_pays_short: Consumers buying vitamins and herbal products

drawbacks.text: The moratorium was part of a broader campaign to stop the FDA from regulating supplements at all; freezing the rules gave manufacturers more time to lobby, and Congress ultimately passed a different bill (S.784) that permanently eased regulation of supplements, leaving consumers without standardized labeling or reliable health-claim standards.

A good-faith objection supporters would raise: the FDA's proposed rules treated nutrients and herbs like conventional food additives and could have restricted consumer access to common supplements; a delay let regulators get the rules right before they took force.
A short delay carries modest direct cost — but it also delayed state enforcement, so states could not protect consumers under their own labeling laws while federal rules were on hold.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: On its face the delay is short and its direct costs small. But the bill was not a standalone timing fix: it was a building block in a successful effort to keep the FDA from ever fully applying labeling rules to supplements, and consumers ended up on the losing side of that broader fight. The strongest defense — that the FDA's draft rules were overbroad — addresses the design of the rules, not the one-sided outcome.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate passed it by voice vote the same day it was introduced, but the House committee sent it to a health subcommittee that never acted, and the bill's final entry points Congress to S.784 — the bill that became the Dietary Supplement Health and Education Act of 1994, which took a broader industry-favoring approach instead.

narrative.text: Introduced November 20, 1993 by Senator Hatch, the bill passed the Senate the same day by voice vote, without amendment.
The House received it and referred it to the Energy and Commerce Committee, which sent it to the Subcommittee on Health and the Environment, where it sat for the rest of the Congress.
The House's final action, on October 7, 1994, was 'See S.784' — Congress addressed dietary supplements through that bill instead, which became the Dietary Supplement Health and Education Act of 1994.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Dietary supplement manufacturers. They got the Senate-passed delay, and when this bill stalled, Congress enacted S.784 instead — a law that permanently classified supplements as food rather than drugs and sharply limited the FDA's ability to require labeling or police health claims.

for.name: Sen. Orrin Hatch
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and steered it to Senate passage by voice vote the day it was introduced.

for.name: Dietary supplement industry
for.role: Manufacturers and trade groups of vitamins, minerals, and herbal products
for.what_they_did: Campaigning against the FDA's proposed supplement-labeling rules, with Senator Hatch's Utah home to a large supplement industry cluster, was widely reported at the time.

against.name: House Committee on Energy and Commerce
against.role: Committee of referral in the House
against.what_they_did: Received the Senate-passed bill, referred it to the Subcommittee on Health and the Environment, and never brought it to a vote in the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a Republican sponsor with one Democratic and one Republican cosponsor and cleared the Senate by voice vote, so no recorded partisan opposition appears; the House simply never acted on it.

industries.industry: Dietary supplement manufacturers (vitamins, minerals, herbs, amino acids)
industries.note: The bill postponed the cost and disclosure burden of FDA labeling rules, and the delay fit into a successful push to permanently limit FDA authority over supplements. Consumers paid with years of delay in knowing what their supplements contained and what the claims on the bottle meant.
The bill pushed back the date states could enforce supplement-labeling provisions, keeping state regulators on the sidelines while federal rules were frozen.
